title: Multiplicative type detected by absence of additive homomorphisms
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be an affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $\mathbf G_{a,F}$ for the additive group scheme [def-sc-gm-ga]. A zero homomorphism to $\mathbf G_{a,F}$ means the constant group-scheme morphism with value its identity $0$. Call $G$ diagonalizable if it is isomorphic to $D_F(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ for some finitely generated abelian group $M$, where $F[M]$ has basis $e_m$, multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$ and comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$. Then $G$ is diagonalizable if and only if $G$ is commutative and every homomorphism of $F$-group schemes $G\to\mathbf G_{a,F}$ is zero. No smoothness, reducedness or connectedness assumption is imposed.

source.place: Theorem 12.18(a),(b),(d), printed pp.237–238; diagonalizable group convention from Theorem 12.9(a), pp.233–234. Over an algebraically closed field the separable closure in (d) is the field itself.

proof.text: Put $H=F[G]$. The coordinate Hopf operations are those of [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. A group homomorphism $u:G\to\mathbf G_a$ has pullback $u^*:F[t]\to H$ and $p=u^*(t)$ satisfies $\Delta(p)=p\otimes1+1\otimes p$. Conversely this identity gives $\epsilon(p)=0$: apply $\epsilon\otimes\epsilon$ to obtain $\epsilon(p)=2\epsilon(p)$. The antipode identity then gives $S(p)=-p$. Polynomial substitution $t\mapsto p$ therefore preserves comultiplication, counit and antipode, so [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor] produces a homomorphism to $\mathbf G_a$. By the affine-spectrum morphism correspondence these constructions are inverse, and the zero homomorphism corresponds exactly to $p=0$. We will call elements satisfying this displayed comultiplication identity primitive.

source.place: Theorem 12.18, opening primitive-element identification, p.237; Proposition 3.6, pp.66–67.

proof.text: First suppose $G\simeq D_F(M)$. The comultiplication on $F[M]$ is unchanged by swapping tensor factors, hence the group is commutative by the affine-spectrum correspondence. For a primitive $p=\sum_m c_m e_m$, compare coefficients in $\Delta(p)=p\otimes1+1\otimes p$. For $m\ne0$, the coefficient of $e_m\otimes e_m$ is $c_m$ on the left and zero on the right. For $m=0$, the coefficient of $e_0\otimes e_0$ gives $c_0=2c_0$, hence $c_0=0$ in every characteristic. The coefficient comparison is valid by applying the tensor products of the basis-coordinate linear maps. Thus $p=0$, and step 1 proves the required Hom vanishing.

source.place: Theorem 12.18, (a) => (b), p.237, with the direct group-algebra coefficient calculation of Section 12(a), pp.230–231.

proof.text: For the converse assume that $G$ is commutative and that all maps to $\mathbf G_a$ vanish. Every $h\in H$ lies in a finite-dimensional subcoalgebra, as follows. Apply [lem-sfb-comodule-finite-subrepresentation] to the regular coaction $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$ and $\{h\}$. Choose a finite basis $w_1,\ldots,w_r$ of the resulting stable subspace $W$ and write $\Delta(w_j)=\sum_i w_i\otimes c_{ij}$. Coassociativity and comparison of the $w_i$ coefficients give $\Delta(c_{ij})=\sum_l c_{il}\otimes c_{lj}$, and the counit gives $\epsilon(c_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$. Thus $C=\operatorname{span}_F\{c_{ij}\}$ is a finite-dimensional subcoalgebra. Applying $\epsilon$ to the first tensor factor of $\Delta(w_j)$ gives $w_j=\sum_i\epsilon(w_i)c_{ij}$, so $W\subset C$ and $h\in C$. All coefficient extractions are defined by the basis-coordinate maps and the tensor universal property. A basis of $W$ is finite: a finite spanning set uses only finitely many coordinates in any basis.

source.place: Section 9(d), coefficient coalgebras, pp.174–175; Proposition 4.7 and Corollary 4.8, pp.86–87; Theorem 12.18(c) => (d), p.238.

proof.text: Fix such a finite-dimensional subcoalgebra $C\subset H$. Define $A=C^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_F(C,F)$, with $(xy)(c)=(x\otimes y)(\Delta c)$ and unit $\epsilon|_C$. Coassociativity and the counit identities give associativity and a unit by evaluation on $c$; the commutativity of $G$ makes $\Delta$ symmetric, hence makes $A$ commutative. In a finite basis of $C$, its coordinate functionals form a basis of $A$. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-algebra-split-or-dual-quotient]. In its dual-number alternative write a surjection $q:A\twoheadrightarrow F[\epsilon]$ as $q(x)=x(a)+x(b)\epsilon$, with $a,b\in C$; these elements exist by writing the two coordinate linear functionals on $A$ in the finite dual basis. Surjectivity implies $b\ne0$. Multiplicativity gives $\Delta a=a\otimes a$ and $\Delta b=a\otimes b+b\otimes a$ by evaluating on every pair of dual-basis functionals, and $q(1_A)=1$ gives $\epsilon(a)=1$, $\epsilon(b)=0$.

source.place: Theorem 12.18(b) => (c), pp.237–238, finite dual algebra and comparison of coefficients of 1 and epsilon.

proof.text:
The dual-number alternative is impossible. Indeed the antipode identity in [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] applied to $a$ gives $S(a)a=1$ in $H$. Put $a^{-1}=S(a)$, so $a$ is a unit of $H$. Multiplicativity of $\Delta$ gives $\Delta(a^{-1})=a^{-1}\otimes a^{-1}$, since multiplication by $\Delta(a)$ shows that this is its inverse. Consequently
$$\Delta(ba^{-1})=(a\otimes b+b\otimes a)(a^{-1}\otimes a^{-1})=1\otimes ba^{-1}+ba^{-1}\otimes1.$$
The element $ba^{-1}$ is nonzero, because multiplying it by the unit $a$ recovers $b\ne0$. This is a nonzero primitive element, contradicting step 1 and our Hom-vanishing hypothesis. Therefore the other alternative of step 4 holds: $C^\vee\simeq F^n$. Notice that the inverse used here lies in $H$, not in $C$ or $C^\vee$.

source.place: Theorem 12.18(b) => (c), p.238; correcting the printed ambient-algebra notation for the unit a.

proof.text: Choose the algebra isomorphism $C^\vee\simeq F^n$ from step 5. Its coordinate linear forms are evaluations at elements $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in C$, using a finite basis and its dual as in step 4. They form a basis of $C$: the coordinate linear forms form a basis of $(C^\vee)^\vee$, and the basis and dual basis identify this space with $C$. Each coordinate form is unital and multiplicative, so $\epsilon(a_i)=1$ and $\Delta(a_i)=a_i\otimes a_i$ by evaluation on pairs of dual-basis vectors. Thus $C$ is spanned by group-like elements of $H$. The zero subcoalgebra corresponds to $n=0$ and has an empty basis. By step 3 every element of $H$ is in one of these $C$, so the set $M$ of all group-like elements spans $H$.

source.place: Theorem 12.18(c) => (d), p.238, dual coordinate forms of a product of fields.

proof.text: The elements of $M$ are linearly independent by [lem-sfb-coalgebra-group-like-independent], hence form a basis of $H$ by step 6. Products and the unit lie in $M$, because $\Delta$ and $\epsilon$ preserve products and units. If $a\in M$, step 5 gives its inverse $S(a)$ in $H$, and multiplicativity of $\Delta,\epsilon$ gives $\Delta(a^{-1})=a^{-1}\otimes a^{-1}$ and $\epsilon(a^{-1})=1$. Thus $M$ is a commutative group under multiplication in $H$, which we now write additively. The linear map $F[M]\to H$ sending $e_m$ to $m$ is bijective by this basis, preserves products and unit by the group law on $M$, and preserves $\Delta,\epsilon,S$ by the displayed group-like formulas. It is therefore a Hopf-algebra isomorphism.

source.place: Theorem 12.8 and its proof, p.233, with Proposition 4.23, p.93.

proof.text: It remains to check that $M$ is finitely generated. Since $G$ is affine of finite type, apply [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs] to its structure morphism, $U=G$ and $V=\operatorname{Spec}F$, to obtain algebra generators $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ of $H$. Expand each $x_i$ in the group-like basis from step 7; the union $T$ of the finite supports is finite. Let $N$ be the subgroup of $M$ generated by $T$. The span of $N$ contains $1$ and all $x_i$ and is closed under multiplication, so equals $H$. If $m\in M\setminus N$, expressing $m$ in that span contradicts the independence in step 7. Hence $M=N$ is finitely generated. Apply [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor] to the Hopf isomorphism of step 7 and its inverse, giving $G\simeq\operatorname{Spec}F[M]=D_F(M)$ as group schemes. This is the required diagonalizability.

source.place: Theorems 12.8–12.9(a), pp.233–234: group-algebra identification and finite generation, after Theorem 12.18(c) => (d), p.238; affine finite-type dictionary is Stacks Tag 01T2.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 12.18(b) => (c) => (d), pp.237–238; coefficient coalgebras in Section 9(d), pp.174–175; group-algebra reconstruction in Theorem 12.8, p.233. The forward implication is the direct coefficient calculation rather than the equivalent representation-theoretic contradiction.

Step 1: primitive p gives eps(p)=2eps(p) so eps(p)=0, then S(p)=-p, so primitives match homomorphisms to G_a. Step 2: in F[M], comparing the e_m⊗e_m coefficients gives c_m=0, and c_0=2c_0 holds in every characteristic. Step 5: S(a)a=1 holds in H, not in C^∨, and ba^{-1} is a nonzero primitive. Steps 6-7: the group-like elements span H, are independent, and give F[M]≅H as Hopf algebras.
